text:
Jordan's week collapsed into a single dense night — September 14th — that touched housing, work uncertainty, sleep, and something more like an accounting of the past month.

The lease renewal was the concrete action: signed one day before deadline (which Jordan reads as characteristically prompt for them), a year at $150 more, done at Groundwork with a cooling cortado, in what they frame as the right setting for the decision. The timing was awkward on paper — a possible Northlight job could mean a commute overhaul and a car — but Jordan had already made peace with this back in August. The reasoning holds: moving is more disruptive than staying, the neighborhood belongs to them now, and a hypothetical job shouldn't dictate a real housing decision. This reads as a boundary being reasserted rather than freshly discovered.

The more striking piece is the third occurrence of the recurring office dream (Friday night, the 11th, in a week where the actual entry falls on the 14th) — the same empty floor, same fluorescent flicker, same phantom typing that's shown up twice before. This time, though, Jordan found the stairs where they'd always actually been and walked out, no surreal flooding or sideways elevator. They're careful not to over-read it — "I'm not going to pretend a dream means anything causal" — but they note the pattern shift plainly: two dreams with no exit, one with an exit.

Work logistics remain unresolved and slightly absurd: Priya becomes Jordan's manager on the 21st, and just three days later, on the 24th, Jordan will take a personal day to interview elsewhere — an onsite for what sounds like Northlight. Jordan flags the awkwardness of this sequencing without resolving it.

The entry's real center of gravity, though, is retrospective. Jordan explicitly states that the job situation did *not* resolve well — they got "parked in the holding pen" — and yet they're doing fine regardless. They credit this not to the job but to a behavioral shift over the past three weeks: telling people the truth and letting them help, naming Dev (the 27th), Mom at the pond, and Lena in the parking garage as instances. Jordan holds two contradictory truths side by side without forcing resolution: they've written "I don't want help, I want to disappear" more than once, and it's still true in the moment they're in it — but it's "no longer the last word." Going into next week: the Northlight interview on the 24th, the new manager relationship starting the 21st, and no clear resolution on which job situation will actually hold.
